title: What is in Samuel P. Langley’s 37 shorthand notebooks?
short: The Smithsonian holds 37 notebooks from an early experimenter in flight. Reading their shorthand could reveal who proposed a design, changed it or saw it fail.
matters: Samuel Pierpont Langley studied the Sun, ran the Smithsonian and built experimental flying machines. Ordinary handwriting in one notebook records Alexander Graham Bell suggesting changes to a kite. Measurements in Bell’s own papers place the conversation at a March 1902 outing. The shorthand could preserve other exchanges that the published accounts passed over.
stuck: The 37 notebooks, digitized in 7,248 scans, mix shorthand with longhand, lists and diagrams. Some entries concern an aquarium. A memorandum names George Wells as a stenographer. Who wrote each book, and which shorthand system they used, still need checking.
solved: Identify the system and hands from repeated, independently readable passages. A dated guide to the volumes and a checked transcription of selected entries, with uncertain strokes marked, would let readers judge what the notebooks add.
approach: Start with pages that alternate shorthand and longhand. Compare the same names, dates and phrases against contemporary shorthand manuals.
Ask two readers to transcribe unseen pages independently and record which words they can recover reliably.
Link each reading to its scan and test proposed dates and names against correspondence, including Bell’s account of the kite trials.

needs.ask: Compare handwriting and duty assignments across the notebooks and the Smithsonian’s correspondence.
Identify the shorthand system and test readings of the same outlines across different hands.
